html:
The New Zealand campaigner who led the drive that made New Zealand the first self-governing country where women could vote in national elections, in 1893.

Born in Liverpool, she moved to New Zealand with her family in 1868 and settled in Christchurch. She joined the Woman's Christian Temperance Union, which wanted women's votes partly to curb drink. In 1887 she took charge of its franchise work.

She wrote pamphlets, lobbied members of parliament and organised a series of petitions. The last, in 1893, carried close to 32,000 signatures and was unrolled across the floor of the House. Premier Richard Seddon opposed it, but the Electoral Act passed that September, and women voted in the general election that November. The story is told on the women's suffrage page.

Sheppard then helped found the National Council of Women and worked with suffrage movements abroad. Women in Finland, Australia and elsewhere won the vote in the years that followed. Her face is on the New Zealand ten dollar note.
sum: The New Zealand campaigner who led the drive that made New Zealand the first self-governing country where women could vote in national elections, in 1893.
